Other Project Member(s): Mohammed G. Elhassan
Poster Title: Three in One: A Case Report of Pulmonary Co-infection With a Virus, a Bacterium, and a Fungus in an Immunocompetent Adult
SUMMARY: This case report details a 61-year-old male presenting with cough, shortness of breath, and rash. Initial tests revealed a triple pulmonary co-infection: coronavirus NL63, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, and *Coccidioides* spp. (confirmed after initial negative results). The patient's clinical presentation, diagnostic process (including PCR and serology), and treatment (azithromycin, ceftriaxone, levofloxacin, and fluconazole) are described. The authors highlight the importance of considering co-infections in pneumonia diagnosis and the limitations of initial serological tests in detecting *Coccidioidomycosis*.

Other Project Member(s): Muhamad Oum, Kamalpreet Gill, Mehdi Hakimipour, Anupama Poliyedath
Poster Title: Reassessing the Need: A Quality Improvement Initiative for Appropriate PPI Prescribing
SUMMARY: This quality improvement initiative aimed to address the overuse of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) in an outpatient clinic. A retrospective chart review of 733 patients revealed that 36% used PPIs for over six months withoutcumented justification. The researchers implemented an educational intervention for physicians to promote appropriate PPI prescribing, focusing on regular medication reviews, timely gastroenterology referrals when necessary, and de-escalation strategies (reducingse, switching to a less potent medication, or discontinuation) when clinically appropriate. The study highlights the prevalence of inappropriate long-term PPI use and the need for more structured management of PPI therapy.

Other Project Member(s): Mason Pitcher
Poster Title: Rising Violence: An Emergency Department Survey Study
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a survey study investigating frontline healthcare workers' perceptions of workplace violence (WPV) in the emergency department (ED) at Saint Agnes Medical Center in Fresno, CA. The study found that a vast majority (96%) of the 100 respondents had experienced WPV, with 58% feeling unsafe at work. While 55% felt current security measures were sufficient, suggestions for improvement included increased security presence, armed security, more K-9 units, additional metal detectors, and improved patient risk assessment. The study highlights the significant issue of WPV in ED settings and offers recommendations for enhancing workplace safety.

Other Project Member(s): Atinderpal Singh, Muhamad Oum, Kamalpreet Gill, Mehdi Hakimipour,
Poster Title: Idiopathic Adult Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: Known but rare cause in adults
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 59-year-old Hispanic male diagnosed with idiopathic adult hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (AHPS). The patient presented with persistent nausea and vomiting for almost a year. Initial diagnostic attempts (nuclear medicine gastric study and endoscopy) revealed a severe pyloric stenosis. While balloon dilation provided some temporary relief, the patient ultimately required laparoscopic antrectomy with Roux-en-Y anastomosis and bilateral truncal vagotomy for complete resolution of symptoms. The poster contrasts the rarity and diagnostic challenges of AHPS in adults with its more common infantile counterpart, highlighting the nonspecific symptoms and the typical diagnostic and surgical interventions needed. The etiology of AHPS remains largely idiopathic, though associations with other conditions are noted.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna Javed, Mahwish Sheikh
Poster Title: From Wheeze to Ease: Implementing Asthma Action Plans for Better Patient Outcomes
SUMMARY: This research poster details a quality improvement (QI) project aimed at increasing the use of Asthma Action Plans (AAPs) in a primary care clinic. The baseline AAP utilization rate was a mere 2%. Using a Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle, interventions included weekly educational emails to staff, readily available AAP templates, and reinforcement of the teach-back method for patient education. Following the intervention, AAP utilization jumped to 78%, andcumentation of asthma education increased significantly. The project highlights the effectiveness of a multi-pronged approach to improve both patient adherence to AAPs and providercumentation of patient education. Future goals involve EMR integration of AAPs and the use of best practice alerts to further enhance AAP completion.

Other Project Member(s): Phillip Kim, Mohammed Elhassan
Poster Title: Understanding Adoption & Utility of Artificial Intelligence in Medical Residency Education: A Multi-Specialty Quantitative Study
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a quantitative study investigating artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and utility among residents across five specialties at St. Agnes Medical Center. The study surveyed 102 residents (85.7% response rate), assessing AI familiarity, usage frequency, perceived impact on clinical practice (diagnosis and time management), and barriers to adoption. Key findings include a high rate of daily AI use (79.4%), increasing adoption with each year of residency, and overwhelmingly positive perceptions of AI's impact on diagnostic skills and time management. The most frequently used AI tools were OpenAI's ChatGPT and other evidence-based AI platforms. However, limitations such as the study's single-center design and reliance on self-reported data were acknowledged. The authors recommend incorporating structured AI training early in residency programs and including modules on AI ethics and safety.

Other Project Member(s): Mahwish Sheikh, Andrew Clark, Aftab Arif
Poster Title: The PHourth pathway in PAH: Experience in the “underserved” Central Valley of California
Specialty Topic: Hospital Medicine, Pulmonology, Rural & Underserved Medicine
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case series of 10 patients with Group 1 Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) from the underserved Central Valley of California, exploring their experience with sotatercept (SOT), a novel activin receptor IIA inhibitor. The study highlights the demographic characteristics of the patients (predominantly Hispanic females), their baseline PAH characteristics (including elevated pulmonary artery pressures and vascular resistance), treatment regimens (including prostacyclin and guanylate cyclase stimulators), and their response to SOT. The authors note that the patient population differs from those in major clinical trials (predominantly white individuals), emphasizing the need for further research to understand SOT's efficacy in diverse populations. The conclusion indicates generally favorable responses to SOT, though one patient required discontinuation due to thrombocytopenia. The study supports the efficacy of SOT in accordance with findings from larger clinical trials.

Other Project Member(s): Ayesha Shahzad, Hamna Javed MD, Celise Nardes Ferreira MD, Mahwish Sheikh MD
Poster Title: Tube, Tear and Triage: Navigating Tracheal Rupture in a critical patient
Specialty Topic: Pulmonology, Critical Care in the ED, Resuscitation Science
SUMMARY: This research poster details a case study of a 94-year-old woman who experienced a tracheal rupture after a difficult intubation. The rupture, initially suspected via imaging (CT scan showing pneumothorax and tracheal wall defect) and confirmed by bronchoscopy, presented with subcutaneous emphysema and ventilatory difficulty. Despite developing a tension pneumothorax, the patient was managed conservatively due to her stable condition following a tracheostomy. The case highlights the importance of early recognition, multidisciplinary care, and tailored treatment strategies (surgical or conservative) in managing complex tracheal injuries, especially in elderly patients with underlying respiratory issues. The poster emphasizes the need for high suspicion of tracheal injury following difficult intubations and the value of timely imaging and bronchoscopy for diagnosis.

Other Project Member(s): Rukhsar Nadeem, Andrew Clark, Hari Randhawa
Poster Title: A Viral Curveball: Rare Case of Influenza-Triggered Encephalitis
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a rare case of influenza-triggered encephalitis in a 65-year-old woman. The patient presented with acute encephalopathy and seizures following flu-like symptoms. While diagnostic CSF findings were non-specific, the presence of influenza A H1N1 and clinical improvement with oseltamivir supported the diagnosis. The authors emphasize the importance of considering influenza-associated encephalitis in the differential diagnosis of acute encephalopathy and new-onset seizures, especially during flu season, highlighting the need for prompt diagnosis and antiviral treatment for favorable outcomes. The case underscores that even in the absence of significant comorbidities, influenza can cause serious neurological complications.

Poster Title: Improving Consistency & Quality of Well-Child Visitcumentation
SUMMARY: This research poster details a quality improvement project aimed at improving the consistency and quality of well-child visitcumentation in a family medicine residency clinic. A standardized Epic template was implemented, resulting in high adoption rates (93%) among residents. The template significantly improvedcumentation quality (mean satisfaction 4.28/5), workflow efficiency (mean 4.04/5), and thoroughness (63% reported major improvement). While most residents found the template easy to use, some barriers remained (time constraints, lack of awareness), highlighting the need for continued training and broader dissemination of the template across the healthcare system.

Other Project Member(s): Ayesha Shahzad, Mahwish Sheikh, Hamna Javed
Poster Title: “No Pets, No Problem? Think Again—Pasteurella Bacteremia in a Pet-Free Patient
Specialty Topic: Hospital Medicine, Infectious Diseases, Critical Care
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 72-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities (including cirrhosis, COPD, and heart failure) who developed *Pasteurella multocida* bacteremia despite having no recent animal contact. The case highlights the challenges of diagnosing opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients, as the typical risk factors (animal bites) were absent. While treated with antibiotics, the patient's condition deteriorated due to other complications, ultimately requiring palliative care and hospice. The authors emphasize the importance of considering *P. multocida* in the differential diagnosis of sepsis in immunocompromised patients, even without a history of animal exposure, and the need for timely goals-of-care discussions in such complex cases.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna Javed, Mahwish Sheikh
Poster Title: CLEARING THE AIR: Boosting Resident Knowledge of Lung Cancer Screening
Specialty Topic: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety, Pulmonology, Preventive Medicine, Medical Education & Training
SUMMARY: This research poster details a study that evaluated the effectiveness of a 30-minute educational intervention on improving resident knowledge of lung cancer screening guidelines. 46 residents and medical students participated in a pre- and post-intervention quiz covering USPSTF recommendations, Lung-RADS criteria, screening eligibility, and management. The intervention, a lecture incorporating evidence-based guidelines and case studies, resulted in an 8.9% average improvement in quiz scores. While the intervention significantly improved overall knowledge, some areas, particularly nuanced aspects of Lung-RADS classification, required further reinforcement. The study's limitations included small sample size and short follow-up time. Despite these limitations, the results suggest that targeted educational sessions can significantly improve resident knowledge of lung cancer screening.

Other Project Member(s): Mareza Tatulyan, Sukhmeet Dhillon, Reema Salim
Poster Title: The shot that shocked the system: corticosteroid-induced anaphylaxis leading to anoxic brain injury
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 94-year-old woman who experienced fatal anaphylaxis after a corticosteroid injection. The anaphylaxis led to cardiac arrest and anoxic brain injury. Despite resuscitation and ICU care, the patient remained unresponsive and ultimately transitioned to comfort care due to a poor neurological prognosis. The poster highlights the rarity but potential severity of severe allergic reactions to corticosteroids, even in patients with prior tolerance, emphasizing the importance of early recognition and management to prevent catastrophic outcomes. Imaging (MRI) confirmed anoxic brain injury.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna Javed, Aftab Arif, Amritpal Nat, Talal Arab
Poster Title: Line-by-Line: Cuttingwn CLABSI With Care
Specialty Topic: Critical Care in the ED, Infectious Diseases, Quality Improvement & Patient Safety
SUMMARY: This research poster details a successful project to reduce central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) at Saint Agnes Medical Center. A multidisciplinary team implemented a 12-month intervention focusing on improved insertion and maintenance practices, including simulation-based training, standardized checklists, daily chlorhexidine bathing, and enhanced transparency through unit-specific dashboards. The intervention resulted in a significant reduction in CLABSI rates, exceeding national benchmarks and demonstrating the effectiveness of a multi-pronged approach in a community hospital setting. While acknowledging limitations (single institution, short-term analysis), the study highlights a scalable model for other hospitals.

Other Project Member(s): Shelby Wong
Poster Title: Diagnostic Challenge in Neonatal Vomiting: Case Report
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case report of a full-term male neonate who presented with bilious vomiting and inability to pass stool at 24 hours old. The mother had antenatal microcytic anemia. Initial imaging (ultrasound and abdominal X-ray) showed nonspecific ascites and dilated small bowel loops. The baby underwent further workup and was ultimately diagnosed with Hirschsprung's disease (HD), confirmed by rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon. The poster discusses the importance of timely imaging and the potential link between maternal iron deficiency and the development of HD in neonates. It highlights the challenges in diagnosing neonatal bowel obstruction and the need for further research into this area.

Other Project Member(s): Andrew Clark, Ajaypreet Singh, Aftab Arif, Hamna Javed, Amritpal Nat, Pankaj Bharati
Poster Title: STOP THE SPREAD: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Reduce Hospital-Acquired Clostridioides difficile Infections in a Community Hospital ICU
SUMMARY: This quality improvement initiative aimed to reduce hospital-acquired Clostridioides difficile infections (HA-CDI) at a community hospital, focusing on the ICU where rates were rising despite overall hospital-wide stability. Using a Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle approach, the team implemented four interventions: enhanced environmental cleaning, real-time hand hygiene monitoring with feedback, antibiotic stewardship, and reinforced contact precautions. Results showed a significant increase in ICU hand hygiene compliance and, importantly, no HA-CDI cases in the ICU from January through March 2025 after intervention implementation, suggesting the interventions' effectiveness. However, the study acknowledges limitations (e.g., single-site focus, short follow-up) and suggests future research should focus on broader studies and long-term assessment, including patient engagement and expanding interventions to other hospital units.

Other Project Member(s): Lea Ann Urita, Shayne Lake, Jordan Thiesen, Samier Alhadi
Poster Title: Feasibility Study for a Low-Cost DIY Ophthalmic Fundoscopic Camera via 3D Printing for Emergency Resident Physicians
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a feasibility study for a low-cost, DIY ophthalmic fundoscopic camera using 3D printing, aimed at aiding emergency resident physicians. The study explored designing a device using a smartphone camera, lenses, and an LED light source. Challenges encountered included achieving proper coaxial illumination and alignment for clear fundus imaging. While initial prototypes proved unsuccessful due to these optical limitations, the researchers plan to refine the design using fiber-optic lighting and improved lens stabilization to achieve a functional and affordable device. The methodology involved iterative design, 3D printing, and feedback from EM residents and experts.

Other Project Member(s): Dildeep Dhaliwal, Jesse Kellar, Russell Martin, Gilbert Moran
Poster Title: Right Adnexal Torsion with Appendicitis, Rare Non-Obstetric Complications in Pregnancy
Specialty Topic: Critical Care in the ED, Maternal & Child Health, Surgery
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a rare case of a 29-week pregnant woman with a complex gynecological history (including multiple ectopic pregnancies and endometriosis) who presented with right lower quadrant pain. Initial imaging (ultrasound and MRI) was inconclusive, but surgery revealed concurrent right adnexal torsion (due to a paratubal cyst) and acute appendicitis. The poster highlights the diagnostic challenges posed by overlapping symptoms and the limitations of initial imaging in pregnant patients, emphasizing the need for a high index of suspicion for multiple pathologies and potentially early surgical intervention even with inconclusive imaging to avoid maternal and fetal complications. The patient's successful recovery and full-term delivery are also noted.

Other Project Member(s): Stephen Howell, Lea Urita, Sonja Joplin, Ezekial Vanstaaveren, Vince Co, Camie Sorensen
Poster Title: Method of Arrival and Patient Experience in the Emergency Department
SUMMARY: This research poster investigates the relationship between patient arrival method (ambulance, personal vehicle, walking) and patient experience in a high-volume emergency department (ED). The study hypothesized that ambulance arrival would correlate with higher patient satisfaction. Using a survey of 94 ED patients at Saint Agnes Medical Center, the researchers found no statistically significant correlation between arrival method and patient satisfaction, nor between satisfaction and time of day, type of provider, or time to disposition. While there was a significant difference between arrival method and the type of provider seen (physicians more often saw ambulance arrivals), this did not impact satisfaction scores. The study concludes that while the results were not statistically significant, limitations such as sample size and potential nonresponse bias warrant further investigation with a larger, more robust study.

Other Project Member(s): Lauren Ma, Hamna Javed
Poster Title: A Case of Tension Hydropneumothorax secondary to Gastric Content following Hiatal Hernia Repair
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 59-year-old woman who developed a tension hydropneumothorax secondary to gastric content leakage following a hiatal hernia repair. The patient underwent three surgeries within a short period due to recurrent hiatal hernia and a gastric perforation. The poster details the patient's hospital course, including imaging findings, diagnostic tests, and treatment interventions. It highlights the challenges in managing Type IV paraesophageal hernias, emphasizing their high recurrence rate and potential for serious complications. The case underscores the need for close monitoring and a high index of suspicion for postoperative complications following hiatal hernia repair, particularly in patients with risk factors like obesity and tobacco use.

Other Project Member(s): Andrew Clark, Hamna Javed, Kamalpreet Gill
Poster Title: Breaking the CAUTI Cycle: A Multidisciplinary Initiative to Reduce Catheter-Associated UTIs in Hospital and ICU Settings
Specialty Topic: Quality Improvement & Patient Safety, Critical Care in the ED, Infectious Diseases
SUMMARY: This research poster details a multidisciplinary initiative at Saint Agnes Medical Center to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs). A comprehensive strategy involving nurse-driven protocols, insertion/maintenance bundles, real-time dashboards, and EHR alerts resulted in a 45% reduction in hospital-wide CAUTIs and a 60% reduction in ICU CAUTIs from 2023 to 2024. This significantly exceeded national average improvements, highlighting the effectiveness of the targeted, multidisciplinary approach. The success is attributed to standardized protocols, enhanced staff education, and reduced catheter utilization. Ongoing efforts aim for >90% compliance with CAUTI prevention bundles.

Other Project Member(s): Muhammad Zahid, Abhishek Karn
Poster Title: Efficacy of Factor XIa Inhibitors Compared to Factor Xa Inhibitors or Placebo in Stroke Prevention for Atrial Fibrillation – A Systematic Review.
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a systematic review evaluating the efficacy of Factor Xla inhibitors compared to Factor Xa inhibitors or placebo in stroke prevention for atrial fibrillation. The study reviewed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published from 2020-2025, focusing on thromboembolic events and bleeding as primary outcomes. Preliminary results from five studies (including AZALEA-TIMI-76, PACIFIC-AF, AXIOMATIC-SSP, and OCEANIC-AF) showed mixed results. While some Factor Xla inhibitors demonstrated significantly lower major bleeding rates than comparators (e.g., Abelacimab vs. Rivaroxaban), others showed increased rates of stroke or systemic embolism (e.g., Asundexian vs. Apixaban). The authors conclude that further research, such as the ongoing LILAC trial, is needed to clarify the long-term efficacy and safety of Factor Xla inhibitors in this setting.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna Javed, Andrew Clark, Pankaj Bharati, Sean Tower
Poster Title: Clot Chronicles:cumenting Cases Of Thrombi In Transit
Specialty Topic: Cardiology, Medical Education & Training, Resuscitation Science, Critical Care Medicine, Vascular Surgery, Pulmonology, Community Health Initiatives
SUMMARY: This research poster presents four case studies of patients diagnosed with clots-in-transit (CIT) at a community hospital. CIT is a rare but serious complication of venous thromboembolism with high mortality if untreated. The cases highlight the successful use of a multidisciplinary Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) approach, combining percutaneous aspiration thrombectomy with anticoagulation. The authors emphasize the minimally invasive nature of this approach compared to surgery or thrombolysis, particularly for unstable patients, and its support by current guidelines. Early recognition and a coordinated team approach are stressed as key factors in improving outcomes.

Other Project Member(s): Dogan Kalamanoglu, Batuhan Cakmak
Poster Title: Improving Sick Day Management to Reduce Hospitalization in Diabetic Ketoacidosis: A Pilot Educational Intervention
SUMMARY: This pilot quality improvement project investigated whether a simple bedside educational intervention on sick day management could reduce 30-day readmission rates in ICU patients admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). While the small sample size (13 patients, 7 intervention, 6 control) showed no statistically significant difference in readmission rates between groups, the intervention was well-received and revealed significant gaps in patients' baseline knowledge of sick day management. Patient feedback suggests the intervention holds promise for improving long-term self-management, warranting a larger study with extended follow-up to assess its impact on clinical outcomes.

Other Project Member(s): Onkar Sandhu, Mehdi Hakimipour
Poster Title: Time is Muscle:es the Red Card Program Improveor to Balloon Time?
SUMMARY: This research poster investigates whether a "Red Card Program" improvesor-to-balloon (DTB) time in STEMI patients at a community hospital. The study retrospectively analyzed DTB times before and after the program's implementation in September 2024. While the program aimed to reduce DTB time by prioritizing STEMI cases, the results showed no statistically significant difference in DTB time (p=0.32) between the periods before and after the program's implementation. The authors discuss potential limitations, including sample size and confounding factors, and suggest further research to explore the program's effectiveness more comprehensively.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna Javed, Andrew Clark, Aftab Arif
Poster Title: Honey! I Shrunk The Lungs!
SUMMARY: This research poster presents three case studies of Shrinking Lung Syndrome (SLS), a rare complication of systemic autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). SLS is characterized by reduced lung volume and restrictive lung function, but its etiology remains unknown. The poster details the clinical presentations, diagnostic findings (including pulmonary function tests and CT scans), and treatment of three female patients with SLS associated with different connective tissue diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, chronic mixed connective tissue disease, and SLE). The authors emphasize that SLS is a diagnosis of exclusion and highlight the need for increased awareness and the development of registries to better understand the disease progression and treatment strategies.

Other Project Member(s): Mohammed Yussif
Poster Title: Improving Asthma Exacerbation Management
SUMMARY: This quality improvement initiative at Saint Agnes Medical Center aimed to improve asthma management by enhancing adherence to guidelines, PEF monitoring, and discharge planning. Interventions included staff education, EMR optimization, daily PEF assessments, standardized Asthma Action Plans (AAPs) with teach-back, and tracking key metrics. The goal was to achieve 95% guideline adherence for medications, 90% daily PEFcumentation, and 85% AAP provision at discharge. The poster details the methods, anticipated results, and potential challenges, emphasizing the importance of EMR integration and ongoing monitoring to ensure sustainability.

Other Project Member(s): Gabriel Allaf, Michael Moya, Jusel Ruelan, Phillip Kim
Poster Title: Faces of Care- Central Valley Mobile Clinic Outreach
SUMMARY: This research poster evaluates the impact of a mobile health clinic in California's Central Valley, addressing healthcare disparities in underserved communities. Key findings from October 2023 to April 2025 include over 5,000 patient visits, with a relatively even distribution across age and gender. The flu vaccine was the most commonly administered. The study highlights the importance of strategically allocating resources based on need, using data to inform future improvements to mobile clinic services and optimize outreach in underserved areas with limited physician access. Recommendations include targeted resource allocation, consistent outreach, enhancedcumentation, ongoing monitoring, and on-site clinical support.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna Javed, Moon Park, William Latson
Poster Title: Point-of-Care Ultrasound Diagnosis of Diffuse Pulmonary Metastases: The Cannonball Sign
Specialty Topic: Hospital Medicine, Critical Care in the ED, Ultrasound in Emergency Medicine, Pulmonology, Medical Education & Training
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 32-year-old male with a history of testicular cancer who presented with respiratory symptoms and a positive COVID-19 test. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) revealed numerous well-circumscribed bilateral lung lesions characteristic of cannonball pulmonary metastases. These findings were confirmed by chest X-ray and CT scans. The case highlights the utility of POCUS in identifying pulmonary metastases, especially in resource-limited settings where advanced imaging may not be readily available. The authors emphasize the distinctive sonographic appearance of cannonball metastases on POCUS, which differs from COVID-19 pneumonia.

Other Project Member(s): Mahwish Sheikh, Andrew Clark, Aftab Arif
Poster Title: PHibroid: A Case of Pulmonary Hypertension Induced by a Giant Uterine Leiomyoma
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 28-year-old woman with simultaneously diagnosed pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and a giant uterine leiomyoma (33 x 20 x 20 cm). The patient presented with symptoms of worsening shortness of breath, edema, and cough. Diagnosis involved echocardiography, right heart catheterization, and CT imaging. A multidisciplinary approach was implemented, including preoperative optimization with PAH medications (tadalafil, macitentan, and parenteral prostacyclin), followed by successful surgical resection of the leiomyoma. The poster highlights the high perioperative mortality risk associated with PAH surgery and emphasizes the importance of a comprehensive, systematic approach to achieve favorable outcomes in such complex cases.

Other Project Member(s): Maryam Hadipour, Aramsadat Meraji, Anupama Poliyedath, Mehdi Hakimipour
Poster Title: Development of a Checklist to Enhance ICU to General Medicine Ward Handoff
SUMMARY: This research poster details the development and validation of a checklist designed to improve the safety and efficiency of handoffs between the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) and the general medicine ward. The high rate of preventable adverse events following ICU discharge highlights the need for improved communication. The study uses a two-phase approach: checklist development (using literature review and expert input to identify key handoff elements) followed by expert validation (using a survey to assess clarity, feasibility, and importance of checklist items). The final checklist will be implemented and evaluated in a quality improvement initiative to track outcomes such as readmissions and communication errors. A QR code is provided to access a survey for study participation.

Other Project Member(s): Mahwish Sheikh, Andrew Clark, Aftab Arif,
Poster Title: Sotatercept and the Vascular-Endothelial Connection: A Case of Thrombocytopenia and Telangiectasia
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 45-year-old African-American woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) who experienced thrombocytopenia and telangiectasia after treatment with sotatercept. Despite initial improvement in PAH symptoms, the patient developed an itchy rash, epistaxis, and increased telangiectasia after subsequent infusions, along with a decreased platelet count. The adverse effects resolved after temporarily withholding sotatercept, but recurred upon rechallenge. The authors discuss sotatercept's mechanism of action and the potential link between its effects on vascular remodeling and platelet function, and the observed adverse events. They emphasize the importance of close monitoring for hematological and dermatological adverse effects during sotatercept treatment. While acknowledging sotatercept's efficacy in improving PAH symptoms, the authors highlight the need for careful risk-benefit assessment and further research to better understand and manage these rare but serious side effects.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna Javed, Mahwish Sheikh, Aftab Arif
Poster Title: From Veins to Lungs: Acute Pulmonary Embolism After Foam Sclerotherapy
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case report of a 44-year-old male who developed a pulmonary embolism (PE) following foam sclerotherapy for varicose veins. The patient experienced coughing, pleuritic chest pain, and shortness of breath after the procedure. Diagnostic imaging confirmed a PE in the right lower lung lobe. The authors discuss the rare but serious risk of PE associated with foam sclerotherapy, emphasizing the importance of careful foam volume administration, adherence to guidelines, and vigilant post-procedural monitoring. They highlight the need for prompt evaluation of respiratory symptoms following sclerotherapy to ensure early diagnosis and intervention. While acknowledging the risks, the authors conclude that foam sclerotherapy remains a safe and effective treatment option when performed cautiously with proper patient education and follow-up.

Other Project Member(s): Mehar Kahlon
Poster Title: Increase PCV20 Vaccine Administration Rates
SUMMARY: This research poster details a project at Saint Agnes Medical Center aiming to increase PCV20 vaccine administration rates among adults meeting CDC-recommended criteria. The introduction highlights the significant mortality caused by *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and the role of Prevnar20 in prevention. The project employed several methods: placing CDC recommendation charts in exam rooms, providing patient brochures, and continuous data monitoring. Results show a substantial increase in PCV20 vaccinations administered after implementing these strategies (46 in the 6 months prior to intervention vs. 103 in the 6 months following). The poster concludes with references supporting the importance of pneumococcal vaccination in adults.

Poster Title: Autosomalminant Polycystic Liver Disease: A Case Report
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 59-year-old woman diagnosed with autosomalminant polycystic liver disease (ADPLD). The diagnosis was made via genetic testing after imaging revealed significant interval growth in the size and number of liver cysts. The poster reviews the pathophysiology of ADPLD, focusing on the roles of PRKCSH and SEC6 gene mutations. It discusses current treatment options for ADPLD, which are primarily focused on managing symptoms in patients with significant cyst growth or symptomatic complications. The authors highlight the limited efficacy and applicability of existing treatments and emphasize the importance of genetic testing for early identification and family screening. The conclusion advocates for routine monitoring of asymptomatic individuals and continued research to develop more effective treatments targeting early disease stages.

Other Project Member(s): Yazan Haroun, Nathanael Reyes
Poster Title: Quality Improvement Project: Bedside Echocardiography Utilization In Clinical Practice Among Internal Medicine Residents
Specialty Topic: Hospital Medicine, Cardiology, Quality Improvement & Patient Safety
SUMMARY: This quality improvement project assessed the utilization of bedside echocardiography (POCUS) among internal medicine residents. A pre- and post-educational session design was used. Initial surveys revealed strong resident interest in POCUS training, but significant deficits in practical skills (identifying cardiac windows and pathologies). A post-session survey showed significant improvement in knowledge and a high demand for hands-on training. The researchers plan to incorporate hands-on sessions in future iterations of the project to further improve resident skills and potentially establish a formal POCUS curriculum. The poster supports the value of POCUS education for internal medicine residents.

Other Project Member(s): Song-ah Baek
Poster Title: Hickam's Dictum: A Patient Can Injure His Spinal Cord However He Damn Well Pleases
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 58-year-old male with a history of depression and alcohol abuse who suffered a spinal cord injury (SCI) without radiographic abnormality (SCIWORA) after a ground-level fall. The initial diagnosis was delayed due to several factors, including the rarity of this type of injury from such a fall, the patient's alcohol withdrawal symptoms obscuring the neurological examination, and a general distrust of the patient's subjective complaints. The MRI revealed a spinal cord signal abnormality at C5-C7, leading to emergency neurosurgical intervention (C4-C7 laminectomy with fusion). The authors discuss the challenges of diagnosing patients with multiple overlapping acute pathologies and highlight the importance of considering less common injury mechanisms even in seemingly straightforward presentations.

Other Project Member(s): Celise Nardes Ferreira Ajaypreet Singh
Poster Title: High Mortality Risk in Gram-Negative Hemodialysis Catheter Tip Infections The Urgent Need for Early Detection
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 46-year-old male with autosomalminant polycystic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis who experienced recurrent fevers and flu-like symptoms. Despite initial negative blood cultures, he was ultimately diagnosed with a gram-negative *Enterobacter cloacae* catheter tip infection. The poster highlights the high mortality associated with gram-negative hemodialysis catheter tip infections (25.3% at three months), emphasizing the urgent need for early detection and aggressive treatment with antibiotics and catheter management to prevent severe complications and mortality. The patient's history of prior bacteremia and DVT increased his risk. While gram-positive infections are more common, this case underscores the importance of considering gram-negative infections in hemodialysis patients with persistent symptoms.

Other Project Member(s): Shiva Hadadianpour, Nicholas Reyes
Poster Title: Enhancing Internal Medicine Residents’ Knowledge of DKA Management​
SUMMARY: This research poster details a quality improvement project aimed at enhancing internal medicine residents' knowledge of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) management. 22 residents participated in a structured educational lecture delivered by a hospital endocrinologist covering DKA pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and management principles. A pre- and post-lecture questionnaire assessed knowledge. Results showed a statistically significant increase in mean knowledge scores (from 55.45% to 85.1%), with all participants demonstrating improvement. Post-intervention feedback highlighted improved understanding of fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, and transitioning to subcutaneous insulin. Future directions include recurring sessions, case-based learning, and standardization of DKA management protocols.

Other Project Member(s): Rukhsar Nadeem, Moeez Sadiq, Shiva Hadadinapour, Nicholas Reyes, Saqib Rashid, Amritpal Nat, Sukhampal Sidhu, Shahab Dian
Poster Title: Severe Macroglossia In Myxedema Coma: A ‘Tongue-Tied’ Emergency
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 55-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and hypothyroidism who presented to the emergency department with altered mental status and lethargy. She was found to have severe macroglossia (enlarged tongue) associated with myxedema coma. Despite treatment with steroids, levothyroxine, and antibiotics, the macroglossia persisted, necessitating tracheostomy and PEG tube placement. The authors highlight the rarity and poorcumentation of severe macroglossia in myxedema coma, emphasizing that while normalizing thyroid function is crucial, sufficient time must be allowed for the hormone therapy to take effect before considering invasive interventions like glossectomy. The case underscores the need for increased awareness of this rare complication.

Other Project Member(s): Sukhmeet Dhillon, Muhammad Zahid, Anupama Poliyedath
Poster Title: "Rethinking Routine Telemetry: A Push for Smarter Care"
SUMMARY: This research poster details a quality improvement initiative to improve the appropriate use of telemetry monitoring in a hospital setting. The study used a three-phase approach: pre-education assessment (measuring resident knowledge and current telemetry use via surveys and chart review), an educational intervention (providing residents with an educational module on AHA guidelines for telemetry use), and post-education assessment (repeating the initial assessments to measure changes). Results showed a significant increase in resident knowledge and a marked improvement in appropriate telemetry ordering after the intervention. The conclusion highlights the positive impact of targeted education in promoting high-value care and reducing unnecessary resource utilization.

Other Project Member(s): Nicholas Gill, Louis Rosales, Kuwar Anand
Poster Title: Abscess Manifesting as IRIS in an AIDS Patient with Recent Disseminated Histoplasmosis A Case Report
SUMMARY: This case report describes a 51-year-old woman with AIDS and a history of disseminated histoplasmosis who developed a painful thigh abscess. After becoming compliant with antiretroviral and antifungal treatment, she presented with the abscess, which was suspected to be Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS). Surgical drainage confirmed a subcutaneous abscess with negative bacterial cultures. The patient‚Äôs clinical improvement after drainage and continued treatment supports the diagnosis of IRIS related to histoplasmosis. The case highlights the importance of recognizing IRIS in HIV patients starting treatment and emphasizes the need for continued monitoring and therapy.

Other Project Member(s): Navdeep Gill
Poster Title: An unusual case of hydrops gallbladder as a source of sepsis
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 70-year-old female with sepsis. Initially suspected to be pneumonia, blood cultures revealed RO ESBL E. coli, an atypical finding for lung infections. Further investigation revealed a hydrops gallbladder (swollen gallbladder without stones or inflammation), identified through ultrasound and HIDA scan. The hydrops gallbladder was determined to be the source of the sepsis, successfully treated with cholecystectomy. The case highlights the importance of considering atypical sources of sepsis, especially in cases with atypical presentations and negative initial imaging. The rarity of hydrops gallbladder in adults is also emphasized.

Poster Title: Quality Improvement Project: Enhancing Career Pathway Guidance for Internal Medicine Residents
SUMMARY: This quality improvement project assessed career pathway guidance for internal medicine residents. A survey revealed gaps in resident exposure, confidence, and support regarding career planning, particularly regarding hospitalist and fellowship options. Residents preferred video and interactive resources. In response, a slide-based educational resource was created, highlighting the importance of resident-informed guidance. Future steps include deploying the resource, collecting feedback, expanding content, and integrating it into residency training.

Other Project Member(s): Ayesha Shahzad, Hamna Javed
Poster Title: The Great Compression: Airway Crisis In Case Of Bulky Hodgkin Lymphoma
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of an 18-year-old female with grade 2 nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma who experienced acute airway compromise due to a large mediastinal mass. The patient presented with shortness of breath, cough, and air trapping, rapidly progressing to respiratory distress requiring intubation. Imaging revealed significant airway and vascular compression. High-dose corticosteroids were administered, effectively reducing the mass size and allowing extubation within five days. The case highlights the importance of early recognition of airway compromise in patients with bulky mediastinal Hodgkin lymphoma, emphasizing the crucial role of prompt imaging, multidisciplinary coordination, and the use of corticosteroids for rapid tumor reduction and stabilization. The successful outcome underscores the need for timely intervention in managing life-threatening complications of hematologic malignancies.

Other Project Member(s): Mahmut Unverdi, Bakht Roshan, Shahab Dian
Poster Title: Mitral Valve Infective Endocarditis Caused by Klebsiella Aerogenes with Septic Emboli to the Brain: A Rare Case Report
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a rare case report of mitral valve infective endocarditis caused by *Klebsiella aerogenes* in a 76-year-old man, complicated by septic emboli to the brain. The patient initially presented with respiratory distress and back pain following a urinary tract infection caused by the same organism. Blood cultures confirmed *Klebsiella aerogenes*, and transthoracic echocardiography revealed vegetation on the mitral valve. Brain MRI showed multiple infarcts, consistent with septic emboli. Despite treatment with antibiotics, the patient required surgery for mitral valve replacement. The case highlights the rarity of *Klebsiella aerogenes* endocarditis and the challenges in managing this infection, particularly due to limited data on optimal antibiotic regimens for non-HACEK gram-negative bacterial endocarditis.

Other Project Member(s): Shiva Hadadianpour, Sukhampal S. Sidhu, Anupama Poliyedath
Poster Title: Hypoglycemia as a Rare Complication of Severe Hypothyroidism in Pregnancy: A Case Report
SUMMARY: This case report details a pregnant woman with severe hypothyroidism who experienced hypoglycemia after a suicide attempt and quetiapine overdose. The patient had a history of thyroid cancer and irregular levothyroxine use. The hypoglycemia, a rare complication of severe hypothyroidism, was attributed to multiple hormonal and metabolic factors including impaired gluconeogenesis, reduced glucagon secretion, and decreased glucose absorption. Treatment involved increasing her levothyroxinese to meet pregnancy's increased metabolic demands, successfully resolving the hypoglycemia. The case highlights the importance of regular monitoring in severe hypothyroidism during pregnancy to prevent such complications.

Other Project Member(s): Abhishek Karn, Maryam Hadipour, Rukhsar Nadeem, Mohammed Elhassan​
Poster Title: A Rare Mediastinal Neuroendocrine Neoplasm presenting with Hypercalcemia and Severe Duodenal Ulcer Bleeding
SUMMARY: This research poster details a rare case of a 31-year-old male presenting with a large anterior mediastinal neuroendocrine neoplasm (NEN), severe duodenal ulcer bleeding, and hypercalcemia. The patient had a history of duodenal ulcer and hypercalcemia two years prior. Despite successful management of the ulcer bleeding, he tragically died from massive hematemesis and cardiac arrest before receiving the biopsy results confirming the diagnosis of a well-differentiated NEN. The case highlights the diagnostic challenges of NENs, particularly when associated with gastrointestinal bleeding and hypercalcemia, and emphasizes the importance of thorough investigation. The large mediastinal mass likely hindered resuscitation efforts.

Other Project Member(s): Sriram Cherukupalli
Poster Title: A Rare CNS Presentation of Extramedullary Multiple Myeloma​
SUMMARY: This research poster details a rare case of extramedullary multiple myeloma presenting as a scalp mass in a 47-year-old male. The patient initially presented with swelling on the right side of his head and gait instability. Imaging revealed a large calvarial mass with extensive osseous metastatic disease, including spinal involvement. Laboratory findings confirmed hypercalcemia, pancytopenia, and elevated IgA. A biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. The case highlights the uncommon presentation of multiple myeloma as a scalp mass and underscores the poor prognosis associated with extramedullary involvement and spinal cord compression. Treatment was palliative, focusing on symptom management and maintaining neurological function.

Other Project Member(s): Hamna S. Javed, Talal M. Arab
Poster Title: Framing Bias and Life-Changing Decisions: A Rare Airway Neoplasm Presenting as a One-Way Ball Valve During Emergent Bronchoscopy
SUMMARY: This research poster details a case study of a 44-year-old woman who presented with shortness of breath initially attributed to asthma. However, emergent bronchoscopy revealed a rare endotracheal anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) acting as a one-way ball valve, obstructing her airway. The case highlights the dangers of framing bias in diagnosis, specifically the misattribution of symptoms to asthma, and the potential risks of unplanned intubation in such situations. The poster emphasizes the importance of considering alternative diagnoses, particularly in cases of refractory symptoms, and advocates for more cautious approaches to intubation when airway neoplasms are suspected. Future considerations include improving communication (addressing language barriers), utilizing direct imaging review to assess airway patency, and recognizing that refractory shortness of breath may indicate a more serious underlying condition than asthma.

Other Project Member(s): Maria Abeysekera
Poster Title: Role Of Genetic Testing For Evaluation of Rhabdomyolysis
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 24-year-old woman with PCOS who experienced exertional rhabdomyolysis after intense cycling. Initial diagnosis was exertional rhabdomyolysis, but subsequent genetic testing revealed McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V), due to a PYGM gene mutation. The poster highlights the importance of considering genetic testing in rhabdomyolysis cases, especially when there's no clear traumatic or toxic etiology, to identify underlying metabolic disorders like McArdle disease, which are often underdiagnosed due to symptom overlap with other conditions. Early diagnosis allows for appropriate management and improves patient outcomes. The poster emphasizes the significant diagnostic delay often associated with McArdle disease and advocates for increased awareness and wider use of genetic testing in select cases to reduce delays and improve patient care.

Other Project Member(s): Maram Cooper, Jasmine Gill, Roma Ramirez-Bueno, Jimmynkor
Poster Title: A Case Report on Methemoglobinemia and Encephalopathy Resulting ​from Pesticide Exposure
SUMMARY: This case report details an 80-year-old male presenting to the emergency department with altered mental status, hypoxia, and cyanosis unresponsive to supplemental oxygen. Lab results revealed elevated methemoglobin levels (37.8%). A thorough history revealed recent pesticide exposure. Treatment with intravenous methylene blue resulted in rapid clinical improvement and resolution of methemoglobinemia. The case highlights the importance of considering methemoglobinemia in patients with unexplained hypoxia and cyanosis, especially those with recent chemical exposure, emphasizing the need for detailed history taking and prompt treatment with methylene blue. The poster also discusses the prevalence and causes of methemoglobinemia, including pesticide exposure as a significant factor in agricultural regions.

Other Project Member(s): Marty Young, Shareen Purewal, Erick Melara, Gullerana Ahmad
Poster Title: A Case of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis in a 20-year-old Female
SUMMARY: This case study details the diagnosis and treatment of a 20-year-old female with Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), a rare autoimmune vasculitis typically affecting older Caucasian males. The patient initially presented with anemia and arthralgias, later developing severe respiratory distress, hemoptysis, and worsening anemia. Imaging revealed cavitary lung lesions consistent with GPA. A rapid diagnostic workup confirmed PR3-ANCA positivity, leading to a multimodal treatment approach including high-dose corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, Rituxan, and Bactrim. The case highlights the importance of considering GPA in younger patients with atypical presentations, emphasizing the need for early diagnosis and aggressive treatment to prevent irreversible organ damage. The poster also stresses the importance of timely escalation of care and proactive communication even when initial diagnostic findings are inconclusive.

Other Project Member(s): Celise Ferriera, Muhamad Oum, Mehdi Hakimipour, Anupama Poliyedath
Poster Title: Delays in Management with Typical Case of Gastric Adenocarcinoma: A Case Report
SUMMARY: This case report details the delayed management of a 54-year-old male with gastric adenocarcinoma. The patient presented with severe gastrointestinal bleeding, initially managed with endoscopic hemostasis, but subsequent delays due to insurance issues postponed definitive diagnosis and treatment by several months. A final diagnosis was made via biopsy after a second endoscopy, revealing poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Despite delays, the patient underwent successful total gastrectomy, and adjuvant chemotherapy was initiated. The authors highlight the importance of timely diagnosis and biopsy in managing gastric adenocarcinoma to reduce morbidity, mortality, and healthcare resource utilization. The poster also provides background information on gastric cancer incidence, risk factors, and treatment modalities.

Other Project Member(s): Don Ha
Poster Title: Influenza B–Induced Pericarditis with Pericardial Effusion and Early Tamponade Physiology: A Case Report
Specialty Topic: Infectious Diseases, Critical Care in the ED, Cardiology, Ultrasound in Emergency Medicine
SUMMARY: This case report details a 35-year-old female with influenza B-induced pericarditis, progressing to pericardial effusion and early tamponade. The patient presented with flu-like symptoms, nausea, vomiting, and near-syncope. Initial echocardiography showed a small pericardial effusion, but subsequent imaging revealed a moderate effusion with borderline tamponade physiology. Pericardiocentesis was performed, relieving the tamponade. The patient responded well to treatment with oseltamivir and colchicine, and was discharged with a good prognosis. The case highlights the importance of considering pericarditis in the differential diagnosis of influenza B and the need for prompt recognition and management of tamponade.

PI's Full Name: When Mycoplasma Pneumoniae Defies Expectations: An Uncommon Case of Severe Pneumonia
Other Project Member(s): Ji-Il Jeon, Andrew Clark, Ayesha Shahzad, Hamna Javed, Mehar Kahlon
Poster Title: When Mycoplasma Pneumoniae Defies Expectations: An Uncommon Case of Severe Pneumonia
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case study of a 40-year-old male with severe pneumonia caused by *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, which manifested atypically with profound leukocytosis, axillary lymphadenopathy, and severe anemia, initially suggesting hematologic malignancy. The patient's condition improved withxycycline treatment after an initial misdiagnosis and treatment with ceftriaxone and levofloxacin. The poster highlights the atypical presentation of *M. pneumoniae* infection, emphasizing the need for a broad differential diagnosis and the importance of considering hematologic complications. It also notes the rising global concern of macrolide resistance in treating *M. pneumoniae* infections and advocates for improved access to accurate diagnostic testing and optimized treatment strategies.

Other Project Member(s): Alina Truong, Aishwarya Vemulapalli, Arianna Crediford, Nicholas Gill, Zunayet Karim
Poster Title: Exploring Hepatotoxicity: A Case Report of Piperacillin/Tazobactam-Induced Liver Injury
SUMMARY: This research poster presents a case report of a 46-year-old female who developed drug-induced liver injury (DILI) after receiving piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn) for suspected pneumonia. The patient exhibited elevated liver function tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin), hepatomegaly, and ultimately required hemodialysis. Liver biopsy confirmed drug-induced hepatic steatosis. The poster discusses the rarity of piperacillin-tazobactam-induced DILI in the literature and highlights the need for further research to better understand and mitigate this risk, particularly in critically ill patients. The case suggests a potential exacerbation of pre-existing liver conditions by the antibiotic, complicating the assessment of causality.
